Colic is a noun that refers to a type of severe, cramping pain in the belly (abdomen). What makes colic different from ordinary stomach pain is its distinctive wave-like pattern — the pain builds up sharply, reaches a peak, eases off a little, and then surges back again. This cyclical, gripping quality is what defines it. Think of it like a fist clenching and unclenching deep inside the body, repeatedly and painfully.

The pain comes from hollow organs inside the body — such as the intestines, kidneys, or bile ducts — when they go into involuntary muscular spasms or get blocked. These organs have smooth muscle in their walls that normally contracts gently and rhythmically to move things along. When something disrupts this process, those muscles contract violently and cause the intense, cramping pain we call colic.
The Two Main Worlds Where "Colic" Is Used
The word "colic" is used in two distinct but related contexts: medicine (in humans) and veterinary care (especially in horses). Each is important to understand.

In human medicine, colic is used in two important ways:

A. Infant Colic (the most commonly discussed form)

This is probably the first thing most people think of when they hear the word. Infant colic refers to a condition where an otherwise completely healthy baby cries excessively, intensely, and inconsolably — for no apparent reason that a parent can identify or fix.

Doctors typically define it by the "Rule of Three":

  • Crying for more than 3 hours a day
  • On more than 3 days a week
  • For more than 3 weeks in a row

The baby is not sick, not hungry, not hurt in any obvious way — and yet they scream. The crying often happens at the same time each day (commonly in the late afternoon or evening), the baby may pull its legs up toward its belly, clench its fists, and have a red, strained face. Nothing seems to soothe them. This usually begins when a baby is about 2–3 weeks old, gets worst around 6 weeks of age, and then gradually resolves on its own by the time the baby is 3 to 4 months old.

What causes infant colic? Honestly, the medical community does not know for certain. Several theories exist: trapped intestinal gas, an immature or overly sensitive digestive system, an immature nervous system that makes the baby overstimulated and unable to self-soothe, or gut flora imbalances. The discomfort is real, but the precise mechanism isn't fully established. What is well-established is that colic is not the parent's fault, it does not harm the baby long-term, and it resolves on its own.

B. Colic in Adults (a medical term for specific pain syndromes)

In adult medicine, "colic" is used more precisely to describe wave-like cramping pain caused by blockages or spasms in specific hollow organs. Doctors often pair it with a word that tells you which organ is involved:

  • Renal colic — This is the pain caused when a kidney stone travels from the kidney down the narrow tube (ureter) that leads to the bladder. It is widely described as one of the most intense pains a human being can experience. The pain comes in waves, typically starting in the back or side and radiating down toward the groin.
  • Biliary colic — This refers to pain caused by a gallstone temporarily blocking the bile duct (the tube that carries bile from the gallbladder to the intestine). The pain usually occurs in the upper-right part of the abdomen, often after eating fatty food, and can radiate to the back or shoulder.
  • Intestinal colic — A more general term for cramping gut pain caused by gas buildup, intestinal obstruction, or bowel spasms.

In all these adult cases, the common thread is the same: a hollow organ is being blocked or is cramping, and the result is that characteristic severe, wave-like pain.

In veterinary medicine — particularly for horses — colic is an extremely serious and well-known condition. Equine colic is an umbrella term for any kind of abdominal pain in a horse. It is not a single disease but rather a symptom of many possible problems: gas buildup, intestinal blockages, twisted bowels, or other digestive issues.

A horse with colic may show signs like pawing at the ground, looking back at its flank, lying down and rolling, refusing to eat, or sweating without exertion. Colic is one of the leading causes of death in horses, and even a mild case is treated as a medical emergency because a horse's digestive anatomy makes it especially vulnerable — for example, horses cannot vomit, so gas and blockages can build up catastrophically.
Summary of What "Colic" Means Across All Uses

No matter where you encounter the word, colic always involves:

  1. Severe, cramping pain — not a dull ache, but an intense, gripping quality
  2. A wave-like pattern — it surges and ebbs, rather than staying constant
  3. Origin in a hollow organ — intestines, kidneys, bile ducts, or the digestive tract
  4. Distress and urgency — in every context, colic signals that something needs attention

The word functions as a noun whether you say "the baby has colic," "she was diagnosed with renal colic," or "the horse has colic." In each case, it names this specific kind of painful condition rather than describing it as an adjective would.
How "Colic" Is Used in a Sentence

• "The new parents hadn't slept properly in weeks because their baby had colic."
  • "He was rushed to the emergency room with renal colic — the kidney stone was excruciating."
  • "The veterinarian was called immediately when the horse showed signs of colic."
  • "Biliary colic tends to flare up after rich, fatty meals."

Because infant colic is so common and so distressing, the word "colic" in everyday conversation (outside of a medical or veterinary context) almost always refers to the baby condition. If someone says, "My newborn has colic," you immediately understand: a healthy baby, inconsolable crying, exhausted parents, and a condition that will pass with time. The medical uses (renal colic, biliary colic) are more clinical terms you're more likely to encounter in a doctor's office or hospital setting.
